extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, mathematical journal editors, and authors of mathematical papers (including mathematical physicists)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance on how mathematical results should be presented, labeled and evaluated — distinguishing rigorous proofs from heuristic/computer-aided work, publication practices (research announcements, retractions), and credit allocation between heuristic and rigorous contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label proofs by type and compute a validity score
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach a label to each proof, e.g.: computer-aided, mass collaboration, formal, informal, constructive, fuzzy, etc. Each theorem could then be assigned a number between zero and one characterizing its validity, to be calculated from the proof’s label, vintage, and the validities of the theorems on which it is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a proposed (controversial) system to make explicit the character and perceived reliability of a proof; the resulting calculations would themselves be a subject of research. Use labels to communicate provenance and method (e.g., computer-aided vs fully formal) rather than leaving status implicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date proofs and record vintage; adopt an expiration notion
rubrics_metrics.description: Published mathematics should carry a date; if after ten years no errors have been found the theorem will be generally accepted. Conversely, if any thirty-year period elapses without publication of an independent proof, belief in the theorem’s correctness will be diminished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dating and a notion of vintage recognize that concepts of proof and standards of rigor change over time. This provides a temporal heuristic for community confidence in long-unconfirmed results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve the word 'theorem' for rigorously proven statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'theorem' should be reserved for rigorously proven statements; heuristic work should avoid calling assertions 'theorems' and instead use alternative terms such as 'pretheorem', 'fact', 'statement', or 'conjecture'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions proposed in the text: 'pretheorem' — there exists at least one set of technical details supporting the sketched theorem; 'fact' — not proven rigorously but considered reliable; 'statement' — has a heuristic proof that cannot be extended without new ideas; 'conjecture' — supported by analogy/examples. Authors should choose labels reflecting the level of rigor claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly flag whether a presented 'proof' is complete and rigorous
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate if something presented as a 'proof' is really a complete, rigorous, mathematical proof, or something else (heuristic/partial/experimental/computer-assisted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested mechanisms include visible flags or labels (even colored flags of differing reliability). Editors and authors should make the degree of rigor explicit so readers know whether to treat the result as established or provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research Announcements should state results succinctly with method indication and independent reassurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Research Announcements (R.A.s) are valuable: they should include a clear and succinct statement of important results, some indication of method, and some independent reassurance of correctness; editors should insist on seeing some writeup of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.A.s are published more quickly and can reduce the incentive for premature public claims; their editorial vetting (requiring some writeup) improves the eventual complete version. Encourage R.A.s as a legitimate rapid communication channel when accompanied by adequate editorial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'Don't Prove, Just Lecture'—do not widely announce solutions without details
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcing the solution of a famous conjecture in lectures or publicity without giving details of a proof (or publishing in unrefereed outlets) is speculative mathematics and inexcusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: wide publicity/lecturing about a claimed proof with no published details, or publishing in unrefereed venues. Remedy: publish proofs (or R.A. with adequate writeup) and submit to peer review rather than rely on publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should publish retractions when errors are discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: When an error is discovered in a published work, the journal should publish a retraction so that all workers may know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely and visible retractions inform the community and prevent propagation of incorrect results. Long, detailed corrections may be appropriate where errors lead to subsequent advances, but retractions must be recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic (theoretical) mathematics is legitimate but must follow interaction rules with rigorous mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic or 'theoretical' mathematics (including insights from physics) is a legitimate part of mathematics; there must be explicit rules of interaction between heuristic and rigorous mathematics so both can contribute productively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristic work can inspire rigorous advances; authors of heuristic papers should attempt rigorous proofs when possible, and rigorous mathematicians should be open to heuristic insights. Cultural cross-fertilization (e.g., physics ideas informing mathematics) is valuable but needs careful labeling and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate credit thoughtfully between heuristic and rigorous contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematician who provides a rigorous proof of a statement heuristically proposed by another deserves essential credit, but one cannot a priori insist that the major share of credit always go to the rigorous worker; heuristic contributions can be highly valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit decisions should consider the relative difficulty and originality of the heuristic insight versus the rigorization. In some fields (e.g., constructive QFT) rigorous work is vastly harder and deserves correspondingly large credit; in other cases finishing a heuristic sketch may be a modest technical task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graded flags/colors to indicate different kinds of heuristic reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple binary labels (rigorous vs non-rigorous) are insufficient; heuristic papers are of different natures and should use flags of different 'colors' to indicate varying degrees of reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine this recommendation with the taxonomy (pretheorem, fact, statement, conjecture). Colored flags provide readers with a quick visual cue about reliability while conveying nuance beyond 'conjecture'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label and scrutinize proofs relying on computational systems (Mathematica/Maple)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofs rely on computer algebra or large-scale computations (Mathematica, Maple, etc.), their status must be made explicit (e.g., label as 'computer-aided') and the community should consider how to verify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of problematic cases (e.g., circulated Maple output claiming to disprove unique prime factorization) show the need for careful validation. Computer-aided proofs may be acceptable but require transparency about code, data, and independent verification; treat unverified computational claims as provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that standards of proof evolve over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts of proof and standards of rigor change; the community should allow practices to evolve and let labels/vintage factor into confidence assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples show shifts in acceptable methods; the proposed dating/labeling system accommodates evolution. Be open to new forms of proof (formal proof assistants, extensive computation) while maintaining clear communication about their status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media publicity is not a substitute for peer-reviewed validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity in popular outlets (e.g., New York Times) does not constitute peer review; claims publicized in the press should not be treated as established without refereed confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating media coverage with mathematical validation. High-profile publicity of unvetted claims is an anti-pattern that can mislead the community and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value intuition and speculation but require eventual rigorous proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal sequence in mathematical discovery may be: intuition, trial, error, speculation, conjecture, proof; nevertheless the end product must be rigorous proof which we can recognize as mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect and encourage early-stage intuition and speculative programs, particularly where they stimulate fruitful lines of research, but emphasize the ultimate goal of rigorous proof and provide avenues (e.g., R.A.s, clear labeling) for converting intuition into established results.
